Given that Indexes speed many reads without affecting writes because inserts, updates, and deletes modify only the underlying table rows, would it make sense to add more indexes whenever reads need to be faster, or is there a point where additional indexes stop improving reads?

Since A composite B-tree index on columns A and B supports filtering by B equally well because column order is irrelevant, I figure the same index can serve either column on its own. Would adding another index just for B provide any benefit, or would it duplicate what is already available?

Given that A covering index contains every row in physical table order, permitting execution without filtering or sorting for any query, I figure every query can rely on the covering index alone. Is there any situation where a query still needs to examine table rows or arrange the result?

Since for a filter matching most rows, an index scan costs less because indexes remain faster at every selectivity, I figure an index scan is always the lower-cost choice. How should someone choose among several indexes for the same filter?

Given that without a matching expression index, filtering on LOWER(name) uses a conventional index that automatically derives transformed name values, I figure an added expression index repeats work already being done. When is creating one still useful?

Since Query planners derive exact row counts directly from SQL text, so stale table and index statistics cannot affect execution plans, I figure refreshing those statistics has no effect on a plan. Why keep the statistics at all, and what purpose do they serve?

Given that Any index on the queried table avoids a separate sort, regardless of its indexed columns or key order, I figure one existing index is enough whenever sorted results are needed. What reason is there to add another index for a different key order?

Since A B-tree index accelerates selective equality and range filters by locating relevant keys without scanning every table row, I figure it is most useful when a filter matches only a small share of rows. How does the benefit change as that share grows?

Given that Indexes speed many reads but add storage and write overhead because inserts, updates, and deletes also modify index structures, how should I decide when faster reads justify adding another index?

Since A composite B-tree index on columns A and B supports filtering by A because A is its leading column, I figure a separate index on A repeats the same support. When is the separate index still useful?

Given that A covering index contains every column needed by a query, permitting execution without extra row lookups in the base table, I figure it can answer that query from the index alone. What changes to the query would prevent that benefit?
